title: Pediatric Visual Acuity: The Clinical Roadmap
summary: Mastering pediatric vision assessment requires a developmental approach, transitioning from behavioral observations in infants to standardized optotype recognition in older children. This guide provides a comprehensive framework for board-certified accuracy in diagnosing and managing pediatric visual impairment.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Importance
sections.content: Visual acuity (VA) in children is the measurement of the eye's ability to resolve fine detail at a given distance. Unlike adults, pediatric VA is a dynamic 'moving target' that improves as the visual cortex and fovea mature. Early assessment is critical for the detection of amblyopia during the 'critical period' (birth to age 7-10), where intervention can prevent permanent vision loss.

sections.title: Pre-Verbal Quantitative Tests
content: Teller Acuity Cards (TAC): Uses Forced-choice Preferential Looking (FPL) based on infant preference for patterns over gray fields.
Cardiff Acuity Cards: 'Vanishing optotypes' (e.g., car, fish) used for toddlers; vertical presentation helps bypass horizontal nystagmus.
Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN): Physiological response; absence suggests severe cortical or pathway impairment.
VEP (Visual Evoked Potentials): Objective measure of electrical cortical response; often overestimates functional vision.

sections.title: The 'Crowding Phenomenon'
content: Single-optotype testing can miss Amblyopia!
Strabismic amblyopes struggle to distinguish letters when closely spaced.
Always use 'crowded' optotypes or full lines for final VA assessment.
Isolating a letter may improve VA by 2 or more lines falsely.

sections.title: Examination Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Observe behavior (tracking, light reflex, head posture).
Step 2: Binocular assessment (Fixation patterns).
Step 3: Monocular occlusion (adhesive patch is gold standard; avoid hand/tissue).
Step 4: Select age-appropriate test (Lea > Allen due to calibration).
Step 5: Check for Resistance to Occlusion (suggests poor vision in un-occluded eye).
Step 6: Near vision assessment (critical for accommodative ET).

content.explanation: S: Strabismus (Check alignment), T: Testing (Age-appropriate), E: Equal (Compare eyes), E: External (Lids/Cornea), P: Pupils (APD check).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: CSM Method: Central, Steady, Maintained fixation is a qualitative surrogate for VA in infants.
LogMAR is superior: Standardizes the task; each letter/line has equal difficulty.
Lea Symbols: Research-validated to equate to Snellen optotypes better than Allen 'Pictures'.
Check for 'Nystagmus Latency': If VA drops significantly when one eye is covered, suspect Latent Nystagmus.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: Low VA in Kids

rows: ROP, Leber Congenital Amaurosis, Foveal Hypoplasia
Optic Nerve Hypoplasia, Cortical Visual Impairment (CVI)

sections.title: Malingering Detection (Functional Vision Loss)
content: The Mirror Test: Move a large mirror in front of the child; they will involuntarily track themselves.
The Proprioception Test: Ask child to touch their own fingertips (doesn't require vision).
Fogging Test: Use a +3.00D lens over the 'good' eye to force the 'bad' eye to see.
Stereopsis Check: High stereopsis (Titmus) is incompatible with severe unilateral vision loss.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: PEDIG
content: ATS 1 (Amblyopia Treatment Study): Atropine penalization is as effective as patching for moderate amblyopia.
ATS 2b: 2 hours of patching is as effective as 6 hours for moderate amblyopia.
ATS 3: Treatment remains effective up to age 13-17 (though less so if previously treated).

sections.title: Special Populations: Developmental Delay
sections.content: For children with Trisomy 21, CP, or Autism, standard optotypes may fail. Use 'Heidi Faces' for contrast sensitivity and Cardiff cards for resolution. Always account for delayed 'processing time'—give the child 5-10 seconds to respond before marking a miss. Objective refraction (Retinoscopy) is mandatory as subjective responses are unreliable.

sections.title: Emergency Signs (Refer Immediately)
content: Leukocoria (White Pupillary Reflex) - Rule out Retinoblastoma!
New-onset Strabismus - Rule out CNS tumor/hydrocephalus.
Nystagmus in a previously stable child.
Fixed, mid-dilated pupil or Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD).
Significant difference (2+ lines) in VA between eyes in a verbal child.
